Lesson 10 · Technical continuation

What happened as the rollout expanded?

The same stores, calculation, and decision—with the specification and reproducible steps visible.

Later rollout · S101–S150 · starts in week 25

← Return to the worked analysis

Read here or present the same material, one step at a time.

Use the same analysis rows

The study uses only S101–S150. Adoption begins in week 25 for the 25 stores with highest baseline rates. Pre-period means use weeks 17–24; post-period means use weeks 25–32. Each store contributes one change.

Case seed: 20261109. All ten labs use the same store IDs and underlying records. Read the shared data dictionary.

Reproduce the calculation

The conventional DiD is (treated_post−treated_pre)−(control_post−control_pre). The guide reports its negative as a positive stockout reduction. The no-policy benchmark equals treated_pre+(control_post−control_pre).

p = world()['panel']
r = p[p.cohort == 'Rollout']
pre = r[r.week.between(17,24)].groupby(['store_id','offer']).stockout_rate.mean().rename('pre')
post = r[r.week.between(25,32)].groupby(['store_id','offer']).stockout_rate.mean().rename('post')
changes = pd.concat([pre,post],axis=1).reset_index()
changes['change'] = changes['post'] - changes['pre']
worked = difference(changes.loc[changes.offer==0,'change'], changes.loc[changes.offer==1,'change'])
assert np.isclose(worked['value'], lesson_result(10)['effect']['value'])

# Verify that the interaction regression reproduces the four-mean contrast.
panel = world()['panel'].query("cohort=='Rollout' and 17<=week<=32")
periods = panel.assign(after=(panel.week>=25).astype(int))
periods = periods.groupby(['store_id','offer','after']).stockout_rate.mean().reset_index()
X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(periods)),periods.offer,
    periods.after,periods.offer*periods.after])
beta, _, _ = fit_ols(X,periods.stockout_rate)
reduction = -beta[3]
assert np.isclose(reduction,lesson_result(10)['effect']['value'])

The code runs after the shared setup in the notebook. The downloadable script includes that setup and runs on its own.

Read the model and uncertainty

The interval compares the 25 adopter changes with the 25 comparison changes using a Welch standard error. Aggregating within each store keeps repeated observations together. Identification uses a common expected untreated trend and no early or cross-store exposure in this study.

Change one analytical choice

Add a hypothetical adopter-specific change at week 25 and calculate how much it would alter the contrast. Distinguish an unrelated operational change from a response that is part of the alert policy.

Connect first differences, weights, and uncertainty

Changeᵢ = a + b × adopterᵢ + errorᵢ; reported reduction = −b

The core interval compares independent store-level changes using Welch’s formula, preserving the store as the independent unit. The controlled change regression uses HC1 covariance. Repeating a store’s eight weekly observations does not create eight independently assigned stores. A full weekly-panel specification should account for within-store dependence.

The two-period interaction regression reproduces the point estimate. Baseline controls in a first-difference model permit trend differences associated with starting conditions. With more periods or different adoption dates, the design and interpretation require additional choices; the present exercise has one common rollout date.

How this case is generated

The shared world contains 150 stores followed for 32 weeks. Delivery time, location, demand, promotions, store differences, and a common time pattern generate the probability of a stockout. Each store-week contains 140 product-days. The generator draws their availability and records both policy paths using the same underlying draws.

The expected alert reduction varies with delivery time and location. Offers are randomized only within the 50-store pilot cohort. Voluntary adoption uses measured starting conditions in a separate cohort. The final cohort starts a selected rollout in week 25. These are distinct studies inside the same business history.

Inspect the numerical mechanism

p0 = 0.055 + 0.014 × lead + 0.0005 × (demand − 100) + 0.018 × urban + 0.003 × (lead − 3) × urban + 0.020 × promotion + store effect + 0.006 × sin(week / 4)

Expected reduction = 0.006 + 0.008 × lead + 0.004 × urban; p1 = p0 − reduction

The probabilities are converted to counts by comparing 140 uniform draws with p0 or p1. Cost is 6 CU per stockout product-day plus 20 CU per week when alerts are offered. These costs are the stated management accounting scenario. The complete assignment rules, random streams, and calculations are in the shared source.

Read the shared generator and analysis source

Compare with the known answer

The shared world’s expected reduction among the later adopters is 4.47 points. The time-comparison estimate is 4.59, reflecting the observed product-day outcomes in this realization.
